results.title: Practical strategies for operationalizing optimal allocation in stratified cluster-based outcome-dependent sampling designs - PMC
results.content: In this paper we assume that after the first wave data has been collected, researchers have the following information available to them: i) the values of cluster-level variables for all K clusters, for example whether the health center is public or private, or whether it is located in an urban or rural area, ii) the number of outcome cases in each of the K clusters, for example the number of women delivering outside of a health facility, iii) the size of each of the K clusters, for example the the number of women delivering in each health facility, and iv) the values of individual-level covariates for all of the individuals in the *K**s,*1 clusters sampled in the first wave. Under the MI approach, the first wave sample sizes of 20 or 40 generally resulted in very close approximations to the optimal allocation, while the performance using a first wave sample of 60 clusters depended on the distribution of the ‘true’ *k**j*s. For example, under positive dependence of *X*1 and *X*2, the average stratum-specific sample sizes using the optimal allocation design was (*k*11, *k*01, *k*10, *k*00) = (17, 22, 15, 26) for Opt*X*1, while it was (11, 14, 15, 40) for Opt*X*3; under the adaptive approach for Opt*X*1, a first wave sample of 60 clusters permits a larger sample with which to estimate the second wave allocation, without oversampling too many clusters from any of the strata, while for Opt*X*3, a first wave sample of 40 clusters is more appropriate. al (2021).3 The adaptive sampling strategy presented in this paper allows for an optimal allocation design to be implemented in practice, by using the data collected at clusters sampled in the first wave to estimate the necessary components in the formulae used to compute the stratum-specific sample sizes, i.e. the *k**j*. When using the MI approach, a first wave sample size of *K**s,*1=20 clusters, or 25% of the total number of *K**s*=80 clusters to be sampled, was sufficient to yield a design that is close to the optimal allocation that would arise if complete knowledge of the data were available at the design stage.

results.title: Allocation of sample sizes to strata | Sampling Surveys Class Notes
results.content: ## 4.3 Allocation of sample sizes to strata. # 4.3 Allocation of sample sizes to strata. 4.3 Allocation of sample sizes to strata. 9.2 Sample size calculation methods. Allocating sample sizes to strata is a crucial part of stratified sampling. * Proportional allocation distributes sample sizes proportionally to stratum sizes in the population. * Optimal allocation aims to minimize overall variance for a fixed total sample size. + Allocates more samples to strata with larger variances or sizes. * Neyman allocation optimizes sample allocation considering both stratum size and variability. * Cost-based allocation factors in the cost of sampling units in each stratum. * Power allocation adjusts sample sizes to achieve desired statistical power for hypothesis tests. + Higher variance strata often require larger sample sizes for precise estimates. * Allocation factor determines the relative sample size assigned to each stratum. + Influence sample size calculations and allocation decisions. + Affect sample size determination and allocation decisions.
